title: Conservation of mechanical energy: trading height, speed, and stretch
summary: Without friction, total mechanical energy stays fixed as a body climbs, falls, or compresses a spring. Solve curved tracks and springs without tracking changing forces.

mass.label: $m$
mass.meaning: mass of the sliding block, in kilograms (kg)
mass.body: Cancels out when converting gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy, but stays in the equation when a spring absorbs the energy.
mass.example: A $2\text{ kg}$ block sliding down a smooth curved track.

height.label: $h_0$
height.meaning: starting height above the flat floor reference level, in meters (m)
height.body: Measured straight up from the chosen {reference_level|reference level} ($h = 0$). Only vertical height matters for $E_p$, never the curve's length.
height.analogy: How many floors up you start before stepping onto the slide.

k_spring.label: $k$
k_spring.meaning: spring constant measuring stiffness, in N/m
k_spring.body: Larger $k$ means a stiffer spring that stores more energy for the same compression $x$.
k_spring.analogy: The difference between a pen spring and a car suspension coil.

grav.label: $g$
grav.meaning: gravitational acceleration near Earth's surface, $9.8\text{ m/s}^2$
grav.body: Sets how much gravitational potential energy each meter of height stores per kilogram.
grav.example: $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ gives $9.8\text{ J}$ per kilogram per meter.
grav.analogy: Earth's steady pull converting height into speed.

ep.label: $E_p$
ep.body: Energy stored by height above the {reference_level|reference level}. Computed with {gpe|$E_p = mgh$}.

ek.label: $E_k$
ek.body: Energy of motion, given by {kinetic_energy|$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$}. Peaks at the lowest point of a frictionless track.
ek.analogy: Cash in motion while the block speeds along the floor.

eps.label: $E_{ps}$
eps.meaning: elastic potential energy $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ stored in the spring, in joules (J)
eps.body: Energy stored by compressing or stretching an ideal spring: {epe|$E_{ps} = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$}.
eps.example: Compressing $k = 800\text{ N/m}$ by $0.7\text{ m}$ stores $\frac{1}{2}(800)(0.7^2) = 196\text{ J}$.
eps.analogy: Energy packed into a coiled spring ready to launch back.

etot.label: $E$
etot.meaning: total mechanical energy $E_k + E_p + E_{ps}$, in joules (J)
etot.body: Stays constant whenever only conservative forces (gravity and ideal springs) do work: {conservation_energy|$E_1 = E_2$}.
etot.example: $E = 196\text{ J}$ at the top, at the bottom, and at full compression.
etot.analogy: The fixed total amount of water poured back and forth between three cups without spilling.

speed.label: $v$
speed.meaning: speed of the block at the bottom of the ramp, in m/s
speed.body: Depends only on the vertical drop $h_0$ and $g$, never on the block's mass or the curve's shape.
speed.analogy: How fast a roller-coaster car whips through the bottom of a dip.

compress.label: $x_{\max}$
compress.meaning: maximum compression of the spring when the block momentarily stops, in meters (m)
compress.body: At maximum compression, the block stops for an instant ($v = 0$), so all mechanical energy sits in the spring.
compress.analogy: How far the bumper squeezes in before springing back.

reference_level.title: Reference level (h = 0)
reference_level.body: The horizontal line where you define [ep:$E_p = 0$]. You may pick the floor, a tabletop, or the lowest point of the motion — physics depends only on changes $\Delta h$.
reference_level.useWhen: starting any {gpe|gravitational potential energy} problem. Pick the lowest point so heights stay non-negative, and keep that same level from start to finish.
reference_level.analogy: Measuring heights from the ground floor instead of sea level: every floor shifts by the same number, so height differences stay identical.

nonconservative_work.title: Energy with friction
nonconservative_work.body: $E_1 + W_{\text{nc}} = E_2$. When a non-conservative force such as {kinetic_friction|kinetic friction} acts, its {work|work} $W_{\text{nc}} = -f_k s$ turns mechanical energy into thermal energy, so $E_2 < E_1$.
nonconservative_work.says: Total energy in the universe is still conserved, but mechanical energy alone drops by $|W_{\text{nc}}|$.
nonconservative_work.useWhen: a track or floor is rough, or air drag is present.

sections.title: Why energy beats tracking forces
sections.body:
On a curved ramp, the slope and normal force change at every centimeter, making $F = ma$ painful. {conservation_energy|Conservation of mechanical energy} skips the whole middle of the path.

As long as no friction steals energy, the [etot:total mechanical energy] is a fixed budget split among three buckets: {kinetic_energy|kinetic energy} ([ek:$E_k$]), {gpe|gravitational potential energy} ([ep:$E_p$]), and {epe|elastic potential energy} ([eps:$E_{ps}$]). Compare the start and end states directly, and the answer drops right out.

sections.note: energy moves between these three forms while their sum stays fixed

sections.title: The problem
sections.body:
A [mass:$2\text{ kg}$ block] is released from rest at the top of a frictionless curved ramp of height [height:$h_0 = 10\text{ m}$]. It slides onto a flat frictionless floor and strikes a horizontal ideal spring with spring constant [k_spring:$k = 800\text{ N/m}$]. Use [grav:$g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$].

Find (a) the block's [speed:speed $v$] at the bottom of the ramp and (b) the [compress:maximum compression $x_{\max}$] of the spring.

sections.title: Break the problem down
sections.note: check all three energy buckets at each snapshot

rows.text: Top: [mass:$m = 2\text{ kg}$], [height:$h_0 = 10\text{ m}$], released from rest
rows.note: At rest means $v_1 = 0$ ($E_{k1} = 0$), and the spring is untouched ($E_{ps1} = 0$).
Normal force is always perpendicular to motion ($W_N = 0$), and $W_{\text{nc}} = 0$, so {conservation_energy|$E_1 = E_2 = E_3$}.
At maximum compression, the block stops momentarily ($v_3 = 0$), converting everything into [eps:$E_{ps}$].
Match [etot:total energy] across State 1 (top), State 2 (bottom), and State 3 (full compression).

sections.title: Plan
sections.note: three routes; only energy handles a curved track cleanly

routes.title: Route A
routes.why: No friction acts, so {conservation_energy|total mechanical energy} is identical at the top, bottom, and full compression.
routes.whyNot: Nothing. Both answers come directly from one conserved number.

routes.title: Route B
routes.path: Use $F = ma$ and $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ along the ramp
routes.why: Those equations worked on a flat straight incline.
routes.whyNot: The ramp is **curved**, so the angle and acceleration change continuously. Constant-acceleration equations do not apply.

routes.title: Route C
routes.why: Equates weight to the spring force $F = kx$.
routes.whyNot: The spring is horizontal, not vertical — and even on a vertical spring, $F_{\text{net}} = 0$ is the equilibrium point, not where a moving block stops.

sections.notUsed: Not needed: the ramp's exact curve shape and the time taken to slide down. Without friction, every smooth curve dropping $10\text{ m}$ gives the same bottom speed.

sections.title: Work it through
sections.note: track the same 196 J budget across every state, then test adding friction

steps.move: Set the {reference_level|reference level} $h = 0$ at the floor and find [etot:total mechanical energy] at the top.
steps.why: At release the block is at rest and away from the spring, so all mechanical energy begins as {gpe|gravitational potential energy}.
steps.whyNot: Do not plug $g = 10$ if the problem specifies $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$; keep one value of $g$ throughout.

steps.move: Conserve energy from top to bottom ($h = 0$, spring relaxed) to find [speed:$v$].
steps.why: At the floor $E_{p2} = 0$ and $E_{ps2} = 0$, so all $196\text{ J}$ becomes {kinetic_energy|kinetic energy}. Notice [mass:$m$] cancels on both sides.
steps.whyNot: Do not forget the factor of $2$ inside $\sqrt{2gh_0}$ from the $\frac{1}{2}$ in $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$.

steps.move: Conserve energy from top to maximum compression ($h = 0$, $v = 0$) to find [compress:$x_{\max}$].
steps.why: At full compression the block stops for an instant ($E_{k3} = 0$), so all $196\text{ J}$ is stored as {epe|elastic potential energy}.
steps.whyNot: Do not drop the $\frac{1}{2}$ in $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$, and notice [mass:$m$] does **not** cancel here: a heavier block compresses the spring farther.

steps.move: What if a rough floor patch did $W_{\text{nc}} = -52\text{ J}$ of {kinetic_friction|friction} work before the spring?
steps.why: With {nonconservative_work|$E_1 + W_{\text{nc}} = E_2$}, friction removes $52\text{ J}$ as heat, leaving $144\text{ J}$ for the spring.
steps.whyNot: Do not add $+52\text{ J}$: friction always removes mechanical energy, so the spring compresses less ($0.6\text{ m} < 0.7\text{ m}$).

sections.title: Energy trade-off during the fall
sections.note: drag height ratio, mass, and starting height; E_p and E_k trade places while their sum stays flat

sections.title: Check yourself
items: **Where mass cancels (and does not)**: [mass:$m$] cancels in [speed:$v = \sqrt{2gh_0}$], but does **not** cancel in spring compression [compress:$x_{\max} = \sqrt{2mgh_0/k}$].
**Halfway down is NOT half speed**: at $h = h_0/2$, $E_p = E_k = E/2$, so $v = v_{\max}/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71\,v_{\max}$ (about $9.9\text{ m/s}$ here, not $7\text{ m/s}$).
**Reference level freedom**: raising the {reference_level|reference level} shifts $E_p$ and [etot:$E$] by the same constant, leaving $v$ and $x_{\max}$ completely unchanged.
**With friction**: {nonconservative_work|$W_{\text{nc}} < 0$} means $E_2 < E_1$ — mechanical energy turns into heat, never disappearing from nature.

questions.q: A $1\text{ kg}$ block and a $4\text{ kg}$ block slide from rest down the same frictionless curved slide of height $2.5\text{ m}$ ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$). How do their speeds at the bottom compare?
options: The $4\text{ kg}$ block is twice as fast
The $4\text{ kg}$ block is four times as fast
Both reach the bottom at the same speed, $7\text{ m/s}$
questions.why: Mass cancels in $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, giving $v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 2.5} = \sqrt{49} = 7\text{ m/s}$ for both blocks.

questions.q: A ball is dropped from rest at height $h_0$ with no air drag. At what height does its kinetic energy equal its gravitational potential energy ($E_k = E_p$)?
questions.why: Since $E_p = mgh$ is linear in height, half of $mgh_0$ remains at $h = h_0/2$, leaving the other half as $E_k$.

questions.q: An ideal spring ($k = 200\text{ N/m}$) is compressed by $0.2\text{ m}$ instead of $0.1\text{ m}$. How much {epe|elastic potential energy} does it store now?
options: $2\text{ J}$, twice as much as at $0.1\text{ m}$
$4\text{ J}$, four times as much as at $0.1\text{ m}$
questions.why: $E_{ps} = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}(200)(0.2^2) = 4\text{ J}$, which is $4$ times the $1\text{ J}$ stored at $0.1\text{ m}$.

questions.q: A $2\text{ kg}$ sled starts from rest at height $5\text{ m}$ ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, so $E_1 = 98\text{ J}$) and reaches the bottom ($h = 0$) with $E_k = 64\text{ J}$ due to snow friction. What work did friction do?
questions.why: From {nonconservative_work|$E_1 + W_{\text{nc}} = E_2$}, $98 + W_{\text{nc}} = 64 \implies W_{\text{nc}} = -34\text{ J}$.
